title: The coal on the lips (Exodus Rabbah 1:26)
hookLine: baby Moses reaches for gold; an angel moves his hand to a coal, and his speech is slowed
tomorrow: who saw God more clearly than a prophet? not who you'd guess.

cards: Plenty of people wince at their own voice on a recording, or freeze when it's their turn to speak. Moses says it to God's face at the bush: "I am slow of speech, and of a slow tongue."
The man about to argue with Pharaoh is not a talker. The Torah doesn't say why. The midrash does.

teach.b: Exodus Rabbah tells it. Baby Moses is growing up in Pharaoh's palace. He grabs Pharaoh's crown and puts it on his own head.
The advisers panic: is this the one who'll take your kingdom? Test him, one says.
Set gold in front of him, and a burning coal. If he reaches for the gold, he knows what he's doing. Moses reaches for the gold.
The angel Gabriel pushes his hand to the coal. He puts it to his mouth, burns his tongue, and from that, the midrash says, came his slow speech. So: why is the messenger halting?

teach.h: THE LIMIT THAT CAME WITH SAVING.
teach.b: The midrash's answer is that the limit came with being saved. The thing he'd later apologize for was the mark of the day he was protected. A neighbor tradition remembers Moses' tongue too.

teach.h: LOOSE A KNOT FROM MY TONGUE.
teach.b: In the Qur'an, Moses asks: "And loose a knot from my tongue, That they may understand my saying." The same Moses, the same tongue, honored in both. And one honest difference.
In Exodus, Moses pushes back, and God sends his brother Aaron to speak with him. In the Qur'an, Moses himself asks, for the knot to be loosed and for Aaron as a helper.
Neither scripture tells the coal; that's the midrash's own gift.

how: The coal story from Exodus Rabbah is often told to Jewish children with the Torah portion Shemot; Moses, called Musa in Arabic, is honored as a prophet in Islam as well.

games.q: what does “the coal on the lips” mean?
o: a fiery warning not to lie or gossip
a limit that came with being saved
a sign of a prophet who speaks with power

games.q: the coal story — tap the pairs.
p: baby Moses puts it on his head
pushes his hand to the coal
loose a knot from my tongue

s: the Torah explains why Moses spoke slowly
Exodus just has him say it; the coal story is the midrash's.
in the midrash, Moses reaches for the gold first
the angel Gabriel moves his hand to the coal.
Moses appears only in Jewish scripture
the Qur'an tells of Moses too, asking: loose a knot from my tongue.

games.q: your friend stutters and dreads her class presentation. she says real leaders talk smooth. what does Moses give you to say?
o: Moses was slow of speech and still the one sent.
leaders are born smooth talkers; that's how you spot them.
skip it; God only sends people who speak well.
games.why: Exodus: I am slow of speech. he goes anyway, with Aaron beside him. the message didn't need a smooth tongue.

practice: Close your eyes and let one limit of yours come to mind, something you'd change if you could: a stammer, a slow reading pace, a body that tires. Don't argue with it for now.
Breathe with it, and wonder, for the length of the sit, what that limit has kept you from, or brought you to.

wordCard.voice: The coal on the lips: Exodus Rabbah's story of how Moses got his slow speech. A burn that came from being saved.

orig.note: Hebrew: heavy of mouth, Moses' words for his slow speech in Exodus 4:10.

carryVoice: Keep this one: the coal on the lips, and the slow tongue still carried the message. See you tomorrow.
